lines.speaker: A
lines.text: How do you know your monitor is really showing ten bits per color channel on Linux? Antoine has a small project for exactly that.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Ten bits per channel. That's the difference between smooth gradients and visible bands, right?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: That's the idea. HDR-10bpp-Display-Test checks a 4K HDR display with a ten-bit color depth, and it's handy for validating the whole chain: the graphics stack, the drivers and the monitor.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: It's a viewer built with Python and GTK three. You start the X server with a color depth of thirty bits, confirm the depth with a quick command, then launch the viewer. There's also a second viewer with video support. To check an image, you open it in ImageJ, which handles ten-bit images, and look at whether the colors come out right.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: An X server, Python three, GTK three, ImageJ and ImageIO, with an apt command on Ubuntu or Debian to get them. If depth thirty doesn't start, there's a depth twenty-four fallback.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: A simple test for a very specific problem.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Exactly. It's open source under the MIT license, and the project page has the full steps and the GitHub link.
